utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning. I believe we still have a rather busy programme until the end of the week, but I hope that we shall be able to bring to the end this whole series of depositions. Prosecutor, are we working this morning in a closed session, if I'm correct? Are these the protections? If not, then we can -- if that is the case, then we can bring the witness right in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fourmy. The witness this morning has only asked for a pseudonym and facial image distortion, so of course he will have to be protected when he comes into the courtroom, but other than that, the courtroom can be opened once he's protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Usher, please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for this witness is J.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Fourmy. Mr. Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning and thank you for coming to the Tribunal to make a deposition. You asked for protection measures. One of these protection measures will be a pseudonym, so that your pseudonym will be Witness J. So do not hold it against people who will call you "Mr. J" or "Witness J" during these proceedings, all right? Now, before you begin to make your deposition, I will ask you to make the solemn declaration which the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please sit down. Try to make yourself relatively comfortable, neither too close nor too far from the microphone. The usher will now give you a sheet of paper with your name. Do not say your name aloud; just say if that is your name or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Translators, please check your buttons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I've had French. It must be a technical problem, obviously. Yes, I can see the smaller red light blinking.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The translators changed their buttons, so that was the problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We won't now have a button war. Witness J, are you feeling all right? The Prosecutor will ask you questions first and then it will be the turn of the Defence. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fourmy. If we could start just about literally one or two minutes in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, again just to be very clear, we are now in public session, which means you're still protected but what you're saying is being transmitted, and so I've already had you identify your village off the record, so to speak, or in private session, I should say, so it may not be necessary, and I would say -- I would suggest that you not then mention the name of your village or any other details about your identity. You can just talk about your village, but you don't have to say -- if you think you need to, but you don't need to say the name of your village, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you were a member of the Territorial Defence, and did you fight, were you on the confrontation line, against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you fighting essentially together with the Croats or the HVO against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that -- up to the point in time that you were arrested, which we will come to in just a moment, did you believe that you and the Muslims -- other Muslims and the Croats essentially were, up to that point, on the same side, if we can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. I did think that because we were the Territorial Defence until the 1st of July, and then we were placed under the command of the HVO on the 1st of July, and we fought together for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, during that approximate one-year period, did you consider yourself either part of or in any event under the command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. Up until the time of your arrest, from approximately July 1992 forward, did you consider yourself essentially part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention, please, to the 1st of July 1993, approximately, what happened to you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was arrested by HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, did you know some of these HVO soldiers who arrested you? Did you know them either by name or at least by sight?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, was this surprising to you, that you were arrested on about the 1st of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you consider at that time that you had given the HVO any cause to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't think there was any cause when I look back upon all that time. I believe everything was fine until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why do you think you were arrested on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, only because I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, were a number of other Muslim men arrested along with you or about the same time that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, some 30 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could you see or did you come to know that the HVO had sort of -- had some sort of record or list of the people that were supposed to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. This one whose nickname I mentioned, Toni, he had a list of men. He was in the same army as I was, so I presume he got it from the commander, or I don't know who from, but he carried around a list and the list of weapons registered and the numbers of these. And then they arrested us and only he would just circle the name and check if the weapon had been seized and would then check it against the number of that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you know around this time or did you hear that, in addition to this list, a local Croat woman was assisting the HVO soldiers in pointing out the Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did not see it personally, but I heard from others that there was a neighbour, a female, who must have shown them the Muslim houses. They could not know which were the Muslim and which were the Croat houses because the residents there were mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, where were you and the others taken who were arrested that day? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After we were arrested, we were put in a truck under a canvas and we assumed we were going in the direction of Capljina, and that is how it was, and we were brought to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that at Dretelj, you were kept in some sort of a military installation with what might be described as hangars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right. Those were hangars or some military depots of the former army, the Yugoslav army. Those were some depots, some warehouses. There were hangars and underground tunnels there, and some isolation cells, but we spent most of the time in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, which HVO unit did you understand controlled or operated the facility, this camp at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was the military police, the boss of which was Ivica Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, because we are not going to spend much or any additional time on this particular location, but you stayed then at Dretelj, at this installation, for approximately 21 days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the end of that time that I just mentioned to you and which you agree, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Next they singled out some 400 of us and transferred us to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And once you were -- generally speaking, once you got to the Heliodrom, where were you kept there and how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: When we got to the Heliodrom, we were put in a school. It was -- it used to be a military school before, and we spent seven days there. After that, we were transferred to the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, were you, Witness J, taken out a number of times from the Heliodrom and used to perform various forced labour on behalf of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right, that's right, that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you please tell us generally what the procedure was by which you would be selected and taken out of the Heliodrom for these labour projects.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Sorry, how do you mean? Could you clarify it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. You were staying at this time, if you will, you were being held at this facility called the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've just told us a moment ago that during this time, you were being taken from the Heliodrom to perform forced labour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I'm asking you now is can you just describe to us the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. procedure or the steps taken, perhaps if I can say each morning or whenever it was, by which you would be selected and taken to these labour projects.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Well, somebody from the area of responsibility would come, that is, from the place where one had to go, comes there, or two or three of them. It varied. They come from a military police who guarded us and they opened the door for them, and they enter and then they pick out men they want, and take them to their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness J, if I understood you well, what you've indicated is it was the HVO unit for whom you were going to work that day or during that period who would send representatives to the Heliodrom and these representatives would then select you and take you to the location where you performed the work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, again during this time, then, were you in fact taken to a number of locations in and about the Mostar area for the purposes of performing labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness J, I'm going to ask you, it doesn't have to necessarily be an exhaustive list, but can you tell us, please, some of the locations where you were taken to perform labour in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to Pothum, next to an old cinema called Partizan, to Stela's, the third elementary school, Santiceva street, Bakijina Luka, then down to a place called Gatavci Kuce, and Rodoc near the Aviator's Bridge, Buna, at Malo Polje, Gubavica, Stotina. These are the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness J, you just mentioned, as one of these locations, Stela's, and can you tell us approximately how many times do you recall that you worked specifically for Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I worked at -- on his line in Stela's area of responsibility seven times, and I went there for the last 15 or 20 days, every morning. Dinko, his driver, would come to get us in his freight vehicle, TAM, that is we called him Tamic, and we would be taken to the automobile association at Tresnjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I understand you right now, you said that the person from Stela's group that would pick you up and take you into the confrontation line was someone named Dinko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Dinko would come to Heliodrom to get us and would take us to Stela's command, or headquarters, as you like. That was his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you know -- you've mentioned simply the name Stela, but did you know whether this unit had a name, or how was it referred to by perhaps you and the other prisoners or by the HVO soldiers, if you heard them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was group ATG, but everybody said "Stela's."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, please, on these occasions, approximately seven times when you were taken to Stela's area of responsibility, did you ever see Stela himself, the person Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did, yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever see and hear Stela interact with or make references to Muslims or the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, they didn't communicate with us much. We would come in the morning, he'd say, "Will somebody go there, somebody go over there," and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase my question, and probably -- I'm sure it was my fault; I wasn't clear. Did you ever hear Stela use any particular terms or language in referring to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: A term -- he called us extremists and, at times, balijas, but mostly he referred to us as extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with this Stela, just so the record is clear, did you hear the name in reference to this same person Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did, yes. His full name is Vinko Martinovic and his nickname is Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell us briefly -- I haven't really asked you up until this moment, but when you were taken to these locations on the confrontation line in Mostar, what type of projects or work were you forced to perform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, these works included from filling the bags, carrying them, making bunkers, then building them across the line, digging trenches, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, on one particular occasion, sir, do you recall that you were working on Santiceva Street when one of your co-prisoners was shot and killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was Puljic [as interpreted] Enver, from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it the fact, sir, that many of the times that you were engaged in this forced labour, you were essentially in the midst of or exposed to hostile fire or an exchange of gunfire from both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. We were always exposed when we were brought to the line to work there. We were always exposed to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that the way, in fact, in which Mr. Puljic -- Puzic, excuse me, Puzic, was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm sorry; his name is Puzic, not Puljic. In connection with him, I can tell you that we were standing in front of the post office. We appeared to have finished our work. In the meantime, some sandbags fell down the wall. They sent him back to repair it and he was killed. From where the shot came, I don't know exactly. He was hit in the head, in the stomach, and in the leg, and we came to pick him up. He had fallen among the sandbags. And then the Croatian side responded and the army side, that is, the Muslims, and they yelled that there should be a ceasefire so that he could be pulled out, that is, his body could be pulled out, and that is what we did. We pulled the corpse out from between the two lines, and then the shooting continued as soon as we had pulled the body out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fourmy. I apologise, Mr. Scott, for interrupting you, but I have to object to this last question. Actually, in our language, it was quite clear that in answer to a question from my learned friend Mr. Scott, the witness clearly said that he was talking about a man called Puljic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's not Puljic. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, my learned friend, through his question, reminded the witness of the surname. Because Puljic and Puzic, in our language, could be compared to surnames like Krsnik and Lasan, not to use an example in the English language. They're quite different names, in other words. That is my objection. In fact, the Prosecutor offered to the witness the name. He actually provided the answer on behalf of the witness. Thank you, and I apologise once again for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krsnik, I understand what you are saying. I think this applies to the second or maybe third question put by the Prosecutor. But I think that the first question was an open-ended one, because the Prosecutor simply asked the witness whether any one of his co-prisoners was killed, and then the witness gave an answer, giving the name of the person who was killed. So I think I must insist once again that when names are given by the Prosecutor, by the Defence, by a witness, that those names should be spelled immediately. In that case, there will be no doubts or difficulties. So your objection has entered in the record, so you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy, I don't want to waste any more time. That was not the point. But the next question -- of course, if I had the correct interpretation. There may have been an error in the interpretation. The next question by my learned friend, the question was: Puljic or Puzic? And to all of us who speak the language, we understand what was meant, because the witness gave the wrong surname and then my learned friend reminded him of the right one. So it's not the same thing. Yes, my objection has been recorded, so let's not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, I don't want to take more time on this issue. I think it's a non-issue, frankly. If anything, it was probably my initial mispronunciation of the name that caused the start of the whole process, and I don't think this is a matter that is so central to the case, in any event, that a leading question wouldn't be entirely appropriate, if there was a leading question. This is simply one particular incident he told us about, and we're just identifying this particular individual. So without belabouring it further, Mr. Fourmy, can we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, it is with pleasure that I will ask you to proceed, at the same time drawing your attention to the need of perhaps spelling names when mentioning names of people or places, so that the transcript can correctly reflect the names. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fourmy, and of course you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, before we continue on, please, can you assist us with this: You've heard this exchange during the last few minutes. If you can, can you provide us the spelling of this man -- the man who was killed that you've told us about, can you give us the spelling of his last name, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. If necessary, I can write it down. Puzic, not Puljic. His surname is Puzic, Enver, and not Puljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how is it spelled, please? I don't think you have to write it down, but if you can just -- if you're able to just spell it, in your own language, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: P-u-z-i-c, with a sign which is pronounced "ch."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, do you have any further inquiry on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I think that everything is clear. We have the answer of the witness, the objection of the Defence, and the clarification that you have just made. So thank you, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, at this time I'm going to ask, with the usher's assistance, that Exhibits 14.5 and 15.2 be put in front of you, please. If we could start, please, with Exhibit 15.2, and perhaps that can be placed on the ELMO. I'm sorry. Witness, if you can look -- whichever is easiest for you. You can either look on the screen in front of you or you can look over to your right at the photograph itself. It's simply whatever is easiest for you. But looking at Exhibit 15.2, can you please tell the Chamber what location that is or what was at that location in 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This is where Stela's command was, depending how people called it. Some called it headquarters. Only it looked different at the time. It's been renovated now. I've passed by here several times and I've seen that some renovation work has been done, so it doesn't look the same as it did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, would you please -- or could the photograph -- or Exhibit P14.5 please be put on the ELMO. Witness J, if you can look at that for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right. I didn't realise we were going to get the marked version, Mr. Fourmy, but if -- unless there's objection, I only have one question about it. If counsel wants to have another version, we can, but in the interests of time, I would simply have him identify it. Perhaps they can -- we have another version. We have a clean version. Thank you, Mr. Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the record is clear, Witness J, I've had placed before you what is, if you will, a clean version of this Exhibit 14.5, just so there are no other markings on it. Now, what I want you to do, and I'm not asking you to make any markings on this, but I simply want you to point to us, please, by way of either -- yes, the usher is handing you a marker or a pointer. Can you just indicate, based on your -- you said you went to work for Stela's unit about seven times, and you've identified his headquarters building. Can you show us on this photograph the area of responsibility of Stela and his unit, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was here. This also was under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So let the record show that, if it's correct, you've marked, Witness J -- follow me now, please. You've indicated that Stela's area of responsibility extended down the Bulevar, which I think by now is clear, Mr. Fourmy, I don't think would be disputed at this point in the record. The Bulevar is the -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. I don't know, but perhaps the witness knows the names of the roads and the locations, and maybe you could ask him to tell us. That would avoid any possible discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, I'd be happy to do that. Again, I'm just trying to move somewhat efficiently here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question, Witness J. On the photograph that's in front of you, 14.5, there is, if you will, an exchange, an intersection that's marked on that map, and there is -- if I can describe it as a major street, a large main street crossing from, depending on your orientation, I suppose, from the right side of the photograph, down and across to the left of the photograph. And what's the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness J. Mr. Seric, you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my submission that it is superfluous to describe a photograph that the witness has before him, so I object to that kind of question. If the Prosecutor wishes, I can leave that for the cross-examination, but regardless of what he has shown with the pointer, if the Prosecutor doesn't want that, I will do that in the cross-examination. Why doesn't he simply draw a line, what he has shown to allegedly be the area of responsibility of Vinko Martinovic? And I repeat, the witness himself can describe the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, I asked the witness initially -- the photo was put in front of him. I asked a completely open-ended question without any direction whatsoever, if he would indicate with a pointer the location. He did so, completely uncoached by me, if I can use that phrase. He marked it on his own. At that point, you, Mr. Fourmy, made a suggestion, and a reasonable one, that I describe the streets or give more additional information about the locations that he, on his own, had just indicated. That is what I asked him to do. I don't think there is anything inappropriate about it. I had not proposed to have this witness mark a particular document. I think the record can be done in such a way that that is clear. Frankly, we have had a number of documents marked right now and I don't necessarily want to have a profusion of different marked documents. We can, if we need to. But I think the witness is perfectly capable of making a record of the location that he's indicated, and that's what we are trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's up to the parties to decide whether they can agree on a photograph which the witness would mark. The reason why I thought it would be useful for the witness himself to name the streets and the locations which he had pointed to on the ELMO is that the substance of the work to be done by those who will see these depositions will be by reading. And then if buildings and streets are described by the witness, it enables the reader to comprehend more easily. That is my opinion. I was -- I hoped we would speed things up but apparently we are slowing things down. So, Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps we could ask the witness to describe what he showed with his pointer - it's as simple as that - and then, of course, during your cross-examination, you will be able to do what you consider to be necessary, including marking the photograph, if you wish the witness to do that. Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy, you have just clearly described the substance of my objection, because that is precisely what the Defence wants; for the witness himself to describe the streets and his impressions regarding the width, the length and range of those, that it should not be done by the Prosecutor. That was the point of our objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seric. I'm sure that the Prosecutor will agree with you and put the appropriate questions to the witness along those lines. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To repeat my outstanding question, the large street that runs to the front along with what -- front of what we are looking at now, the health centre, you said this a moment ago, what is the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a few moments ago, you indicated, and is it correct, that the area of responsibility on the Bulevar extended to the left, to the intersection which is visible on Exhibit 14.5? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to direct your attention to the 17th of September, Witness J, and those photographs can be withdrawn at this time. Can you tell us -- and not all at one time, we will take it in pieces. Tell us what happened on the 17th of September, starting with, of course, the beginning or early part of the day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: On the 17th of September 1993, early in the morning, about 6.00, 6.30, I don't know exactly, at the gymnasium in the Heliodrom, Dinko came to fetch us. There were about 30 of us in the group and we were taken in the direction of the town of Mostar. Four men were left at Zovnica, at a private house. Then we were taken to Stela's headquarters or command. After that, there was quite a large group of soldiers there already, and Stela was walking around, and on one occasion he said that four men should be selected. Jasmin Jazvin, Enes Pajo, Edo Tucakovic and Jasar Gadzo. The four of them went to the basement of that building, they dressed and they came back out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness J, forgive me for interrupting you. To follow Mr. Fourmy's suggestion, if you can help us, please, can you spell the last names of those four men you just identified, or the men you just identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Let me mention Jazvin first. J-a-z-v-i-n. And his first name, J-a-s-m-i-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And the next individual, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: T-u-c-a-k-o-v-i-c, first name E-d-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the third individual, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: P-a-j-o, first name E-n-e-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: If necessary, I can give you name, spell the fourth name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: G-a-d-z-o, first name J-a-s-a-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness J. Now, before the -- before you got to this point -- we can stop there for a moment, where these four men were selected, where -- excuse me, just let me look at your testimony for a second. All right, I'm sorry, you already mentioned -- this is at Stela's, you were taken to Stela's headquarters. Who -- can you identify the particular individual who made the selection of the four people you just named?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: His name was Ernest. He's a dark guy with a black beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did this Ernest have a nickname that he was frequently called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. We called him Brada, meaning beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell the -- can you tell the Chamber whether, when all this is happening that you described for us in the last few minutes, was Stela present at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. He was there behind, near, around the building but not exactly where we were lined up. He was walking around the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, forgive me for being a little bit out of sequence here, but let me go back and pick up one additional item that we missed. You said that some -- I think you said that some of the prisoners were split off, if you will, to go work in a garage as mechanics on some cars. If you said that, I'm sorry, I didn't -- don't recall hearing it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. It was a group of five or six men who were always working for Stela. There was a garage right next to the entrance to the building and they repaired cars and prepared them for painting and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. My apology, Mr. Fourmy, if I just didn't remember if that had been covered or not. I take -- I took us on a bit of a detour, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back to the selection of the four soldiers. Did one of these four then collapse or faint, if you will, on being selected and put into a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. It was Enes Pajo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened after that? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: When he fainted, there was a lot of commotion, and then Mr. Stela shouted that he should be replaced by someone else, as we were lined up over there in front of the building, and then he chose me, Ernest chose me. And then I put on a camouflage uniform and joined the three remaining men. I was the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did all four of you then at that point have on a camouflage military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you, the group of you four, were you given anything else around this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. After that, we were given wooden rifles which looked like real ones but they were made out of wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After that, we were told to clean up, to clean the weapons of the soldiers that were there. In the meantime, the others went on some other assignment, the people who stayed behind us, and we stayed on to clean the weapons until the time came for us to leave. So after a short while, we went together with Ernest in a car. We called it a Fico Kombi, a small van with a PAM on it, an anti-aircraft gun on it, and we went to the line down there, the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the part of the line or the building where you were taken at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know the area too well, but they called it the emergency, and we went to the basement of that emergency building and Mr. Stela was there in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What street was this emergency centre, as you call it, located on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is -- I don't know the exact name of the street, but it is in the direction when you go from the Rondo towards the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said a moment ago that when you arrived there, somebody else was already there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the what you've described as the emergency centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Down there, in the basement, Stela was waiting for us where -- and Ernest brought us there, and he took us to Stela's, and there were another two or three soldiers with him, I don't know their names, and Stela told us what our assignment was, what was going to happen that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He told us that there would be an operation that day at 12.00 and that we would be the men who would go in front of them, because they don't know exactly -- they didn't know exactly -- they knew the building but they didn't know the exact positions of the army, and they wanted to see where the shooting was coming from, for them to be able to respond, and we would go in front of the group, the group consisting of about ten men who would be following us. And he told us that the operation would start with shelling at 12.00, it would go on for some 15 minutes, and after that, a tank would come from the direction of the Rondo, which would stop there in front of this emergency building, or whatever they called it, because there was a wall made of sandbags that we had made previously there, and this would be removed, and then the tank would come and would fire three or four shells - and that in fact happened - after which we should follow the tank to the crossroads. It would stop there, and we should go on and run across the road. After that, we should lie down in front of the building which the army held, and then that they would continue the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, let me stop you there, please. Just by point of clarification on a couple of things you've just told us. When you say, and again just now, the positions or the building which the army held, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which army are you referring to in that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you being used then, you and the three other men -- to use the phrase that's been referred to during and since the war, did you understand that you were being used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. I've already said that he had told us to go because they did not know where Armija's men were exactly, and that we should walk in front of them so that they could simply fire at us and thus they would establish where that fire was coming from, that is, where they were, and proceed with their action. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness J, before I ask you - and we're coming to the end of your testimony - before I ask you to just tell us the rest of the story, if you will, what happened after this, going back to the instructions you received, you've told us, from Stela, did he say anything that might happen or would happen if the mission succeeded, or the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Stela told us, when this is over, if we're successful and if all goes all right, that he then guarantees that he will release us within 48 hours, so that we could go home if we wanted to, or away if we wanted to, or join his unit if we wanted to. And then his other soldiers who were there said, "Just be sure, if he promises something, that is how it will be."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Witness J, will you just then tell us what happened next up until the end of this event, the end of this time when you and the others were being used in the manner you've described. Just tell us in your own words the rest of the story.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. From the basement, we went to a garage, and there we were separated from those others. We were not allowed to see those others. I don't know why. And then Ernest came and brought a backpack and gave it to this Sarajevan, to Jasar Gadzo, and two small bags which he gave to Jasmin and Edo, and then he ordered them to fill them with stones. After that, he found a small half-litre bottle for the motor oil and told him to put it in his pocket and said, "This is your Motorola. When you cross over there and do your mission, then call me." Well, a few minutes passed by and then we went to the lower part of that health centre. There was a side entrance to it. And there we awaited for the tank with the rest of Stela's soldiers, those who were to move on first. And at 12.00, the shelling started and lasted for some 15 or 20 minutes, and as it stopped, the tank came up from the direction of Rondo. Meanwhile, those others, the inmates, had removed the bags that were on the street so that the tank could pass through, and then it fired three or four shells and set off. And they told us -- that is, they again came to us, I mean, the tank. The tank came back to the entrance where we were, and then we were told to come out and start off to the mission, to the task that we had been assigned. And that's how it was. We ran alongside the tank up to the fountain, and there the tank stopped and we managed to run across by the fountain and across the Bulevar and reach the side where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was and we went down on the ground. And then the infantry exchange of fire started and shelling of everything. There were all sorts of things there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you, Witness J. Forgive me. And once you got to the other side of the street, what did you do and what was your situation at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, we went down to the ground then, and as soon as we -- that is, the moment we heard the first rifle shot, we simply laid down, because the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not spot us. So that we laid down on the ground the moment the first rifle fired, and then this fire started. However, soldiers who were from Stela's group, they stood behind the fountain, and then so it went on, and we were there throughout the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you think was going to happen to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, what could we think? We were waiting for the -- awaiting death, and I was really looking forward to it and I was hoping for the right death, to be hit in the right place, that is, not to be severely wounded, because I don't think anybody would have come to my rescue there and nobody could come there to get me out. So whoever tried to come to your rescue would be finished, from either side. So all I did was pray for death, that is, to be killed on the spot. But it stopped, and when this gunfire died down, Stela's soldiers withdrew. And Jasmin Jazvin -- we were quite near the entrance to this building held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he made it to the entrance, and we heard some talk, some voices there. And at some point he simply jumped up and rushed into the building held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there a soldier met him. But he had already warned him before that that he was a prisoner and threw at him his rifle and told him not to fire at him. At that moment, he cried out to get away, to get down to the cellar of the building. And when I heard that, I also pushed those other two and told them that we also had to get in there, and if we make it, we make it. And that's how it was. With the rest of us, we crossed over and we got away with it. And he asked us, "Are there any more of you?" And we said, "No. Only the four of us." And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness J. Mr. Fourmy, we have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I wonder if perhaps -- Mr. Krsnik, Mr. Seric, what do you think? Should we make a break now, a 20-minute break, and then begin your cross-examination? Would you agree with this? Yes? Very well. In that case, we shall resume at 10 minutes to 11.00. The session is adjourned. Witness, please do not move. Wait for the usher to take you out of the courtroom. Stay in your place. Thank you very much. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Yes, Witness J, the Defence will now ask you some questions. It will be, yes, Madam Lasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness J.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: I'm Visnja Drenski Lasan, lawyer and co-counsel for the accused Mladen Naletilic, and I will ask you only a few questions relative to your testimony today. Tell us: Before your testimony today, you already gave -- made a statement to our colleagues from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: According to my information, it was on the 9th of December 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: And you remember what you said in that statement, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I said what I told about today.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: And all that you said today and what you stated on that occasion is true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Merely for clarification for the today's record, I will ask you a few questions which have to do with the initial part of your today's testimony. When asked by the Prosecutor, that is what you said in your statement, you said that you were taken to the camp at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: You also told us today, and that is what your statement says, that the Dretelj camp was commanded by the HVO military police, and you mentioned the name of the person who was the camp administrator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: And for the transcript, could you please repeat the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Ivica Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Could you please spell it out, for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I-v-i-c-a, last name K-r-a-l-j-e-v-i-c with a diacritic mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: You told us, and that is what your first statement says also, that after that, you were taken to the camp at Heliodrom near Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know what the locality is called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It's called Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: You also said today that this camp was also under the command of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the camp administrator of the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: You also said that from the camp at Heliodrom, you were taken to work at different places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: You also said that various persons came to the camp and then you told us about the procedure which led up to your being taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: You also said something about it in your first statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that I should like to ask the usher to show the witness the text of his statement of 9th December 1998, page 2, the passage marked in blue. And I also have copies in English and Croatian for the Court and for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the text be put on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I only wish to show it to the witness. Perhaps there will be no need to tender it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the text in question be put on the ELMO, please, for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 2 of the statement. The usher asked me if, in view of the protection of the witness, if this fragment which I want to show, I do not think that it will affect his safety and it has nothing to do with him. I mean, it does not address any of his particulars.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is a protected -- this document is confidential. It does say his name on the second page, and we cannot show it on the ELMO. We can show him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. It doesn't have to be put there, only to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any objections if the statement is not put on the ELMO? Then I believe the witness is protected. Or do you have any other objection, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, we have no objection to it not being put on the ELMO. I think that was primarily, if I understood correctly, for the benefit perhaps of the interpreters. But I agree that if the entire document, or at least parts of the document, become shown on the ELMO, it would compromise the witness. I think that -- well, I think the cross-examination can be done in such a way, hopefully using the document, without disclosing the document itself. I have some other concerns. The reason I'm hesitating, Mr. Fourmy, and I apologise, I have some other concerns about the way in which these statements are coming into the record, but it's something we can address more generally. I don't want to take the time now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D1/10.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: In this paragraph that has been highlighted and shown to you now, it says that you arrived at the Heliodrom, that the military police of the HVO was in charge of that camp. You said that you don't know who the commander was. You said that you were frequently taken to do forced labour in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Could you find the following sentences in that text that has been marked for you: "Whichever battalion needed the labour would --"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Do you want me to list --

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: No. No, no. Just this sentence I am reading to you now. The previous sentence says, "... the surroundings of Mostar," and then comes the following sentence, beginning with the word, "Whichever battalion..." Can you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: "Whichever battalion needed labour, that battalion would send a truck to the hangar at Heliodrom." Those were battalions of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Could you clarify for us, please: These HVO battalions that came to the Heliodrom to fetch labour, manpower, they were not stationed at Heliodrom, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: They were at some other locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. They were in their respective areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: I see. Then comes the sentence: "Then the military police from the Heliodrom would pick us out"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Sometimes it would be the military police, sometimes the people who came to fetch us; the military police and the people who came with trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Tell us exactly the procedure of selection amongst you who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The door would be open. Either the military police would come in or somebody who came from his own area of responsibility, and he would select the number of people he needed. There were quite a number of us there, so he would select people at will.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: In view of all that you said, can we conclude that you couldn't be taken to do forced labour unless the military police at the Heliodrom knew about it and approved it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. They would have to open the door, regardless of who came, because they guarded us, the military police. Sometimes they would select us and sometimes these soldiers who came from their areas of responsibility would select us, in the presence of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: So the selection of individuals, that is, whether it would be prisoner A or prisoner B or prisoner C, that this selection would sometimes be done by the person who came to fetch you and sometimes by the military police, but the military police was always there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. They guarded us. They had to open the hangar, let them in, and they had to be aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: So can you confirm what I have just said, for the record, as we have been told that we are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Could you wait for me to finish the question before you give your answer, because of the interpretation, so as not to have any overlapping. You said today that as a member of the HVO, you were arrested on the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In my village, my native village.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: Just a moment. I am not interested in the name, but the precise location: the street, the house, at a front line, in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this. Maybe I misunderstood the question, but there is no reason for him to give an address or a house. He stated in private session where he's from, his village, and this is not necessary. It's only identifying the witness and it's simply irrelevant for any proper cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Lasan, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question did not require an address. I cautioned the witness that I was not interested in names. All I was interested in was the actual location. Was it in a house, in front of the house, on the road, in the woods? This can in no way compromise the witness's protection, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Lasan. Perhaps I would suggest we go into private session for a few minutes, and that would give the witness greater freedom to answer your question. Because if the answer is that he was arrested in the street, there's a risk of embarking upon something that could permit identification. But I think, in view of the area, the circumstances, it is quite easy to identify people. So if you agree, we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LASAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you think that would be a better idea, but in my opinion it is not necessary. But out of caution, maybe we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Lasan. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 12 page 1532 redacted, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm attorney Branko Seric, representing Vinko Martinovic. Witness J, do you remember when you arrived at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You mean from Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The 21st of July 1993, in the evening. I don't know exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor, virtually in the same response, you said that you went to Stela's six or seven times but you also said that for the last 15 days, you were taken there every day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken there, but not just I but some others with me. We went to work in the automotive association for Nikica Kresic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, then, where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: To the automotive, motoring association. I didn't know Mostar very well before. I became acquainted with it while I was in the camp there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Why are you linking that with Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: What do you mean linking? Because Dinko [LiveNote originally read in error "Vinko"] came to the Heliodrom, and he took us as a group, and when we reached Stela's, then this one would take us over for the motoring association, the four of us, and the others would stay for Stela, and that repeated itself for 15 or 20 days at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 17th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I only intervene, I think, for your benefit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I'm wrong, I'm sure I'll be corrected, but on line 20, I believe he said because Vinko came to the Heliodrom. I would understand that the witness said Dinko. That may be important to you but I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dinko, Dinko, I'm sorry, not Vinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Precisely so. But let me go on. Before the 17th of September, when you were placed under the authority of Vinko Martinovic's unit, were you taken to the separation line at Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I said already, six or seven times I worked for Stela at the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Is this date the 17th of September 1993 important for you in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Something in particular? Well, what happened was what I have just told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What were you wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I had some shoes on, shoes I found when I went to do labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where did you find them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In a house, in an abandoned house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where is that abandoned house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm afraid I just couldn't tell you now. I couldn't explain, because I worked almost every day. And where exactly I found them, I'm unable to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you were taken to work for the first time for Vinko Martinovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't tell you exactly when it was that I was taken for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness, as we didn't have other technical possibilities, show the witness a copy of photograph Exhibit 14.5. The original was used this morning, so could I have the original, please, which is already in the file, which was shown to the witness this morning without any markings, 14.5? Mr. Usher, could you give copies to the Prosecution, the Court and the Registrar? A copy, because I would like to use the copy for marking purposes, so then it will be a Defence exhibit. After the witness has marked it, we would like to tender it as a Defence exhibit, if my learned friends have no objection, though the copy is black and white, but I think that shouldn't cause any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that is quite an acceptable way to proceed, Mr. Seric. Madam Registrar, perhaps you could give us a number for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The new exhibit that will be marked for the Defence will be D2/3. But just to clarify for the record, they are using OTP Exhibit P14.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you be kind enough to use the marker and to draw what you pointed to the Prosecutor this morning, that is, the area of responsibility of Vinko Martinovic's unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You haven't finished the part to the back of the photograph held by this unit, or perhaps you don't know. Do you understand what I mean, I hope?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what you're saying. I think the end of this building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Just draw a line horizontally where you think this should be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The end of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Just draw a line, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And to the right. No, that's to the left. To the right, you have a line you've already drawn. Further up, at the end of the photograph, where does that line end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Well, just draw a line as you think best.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I have, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, you have not finished it. You haven't finished the line. To the right, upper right. There, there, where is the end, there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This building here. That is the end of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Just draw a line to the left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This is the roof. So to avoid any confusion, I'm drawing the line like this, so as not to go deeper inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Please draw a line across the building. We see that this is an aerial photograph, so please draw a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, I'm sorry. If I can -- Witness, I'm going to interrupt you. Sorry, but if I don't -- Sorry, Mr. Fourmy, but if I don't interrupt, then it may be too late, and I apologise for any discourtesy to anyone in the courtroom. Mr. Fourmy, I'm afraid that I have now the same objection that apparently I was the victim of, if I may say that, in the direct examination. I understand completely that Mr. Seric wants certain marks to be put on the map. I understand that. I have no objection to that. But I think now we've reached the point where it's being too directive. Mr. Seric is giving too much direction as to the lines that he wants. The witness has already drawn the lines that I think he can draw, and I think once he's completed that, he should not be coached or encouraged to draw additional lines. I think he's given his full answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for any interruption - I agree with my learned friend - or objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So as far as you are concerned, have you finished marking the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That is as far as his area of responsibility is concerned that I went to, and as far as I know. That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is behind this building on the right-hand side, as the last one, so that you couldn't mark the line because of the roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This building, this last building up there? This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes. What's behind that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know what it was. There were some rooms there under a flat roof and there were rifles positioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Underneath that building, the one on the right-hand side that you said had a flat roof, did that mark the end of the area of responsibility of the unit led by Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know I came there. Whether that was the end, I don't know. I came here, and over here too, and here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Fourmy, could we keep this photograph in front of the witness for a while? Because we will need it again during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said a while ago that even before the 17th of September, you came to work near the separation line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that place on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, it's this. This was called the 3rd Primary School. Somewhere in this direction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking in this area that you marked as manned by Vinko Martinovic's unit along the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I went from there -- no, sorry. Can you clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: A while ago you marked -- look at the photograph. You marked the area manned on the separation line by the Vinko Martinovic unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And where did you work within that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Oh, you mean within that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, then inside here in this building, then here, in this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you work inside those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you work in front of those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In front of the buildings, not here. Only inside, and the yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And on those occasions when you worked there, did you ever witness a conflict, an exchange of fire, between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, there would be some intermittent fire, a bullet here and there; not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you personally ever at risk on those occasions when there was fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, we had to seek shelter the moment the fire starts, because what we were doing there was reinforcing the rifle positions and suchlike so that as soon as a rifle would open fire, we had to get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you see where that fire came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see that, and we didn't watch, nothing. There were only those slots for the rifles. You couldn't really have much visibility, and you only had to work. We couldn't look through those slots.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you have a look at this photograph once again and tell us: Where were the units of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Here, along this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Next to the line that you've just drawn, can you somehow indicate -- to indicate that those were the ABiH positions, put "1."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You want me to write "1"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Where? On which side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Well -- no, here it's too dark, so you can't see it. Here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you -- now, and at the end of the right-hand line that you marked, will you please put also number "1."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Here, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, put number "2" to indicate the areas that you worked, or rather, the buildings. You were shown them a moment ago, so will you please put "2."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You mean when I worked for Stela?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: And this one here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you show me - you don't have to write anything - where was the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It's here, that building over there. That's what they told us: the health centre. And this one they called emergency. Whether that was also a part of the health centre, I don't know, but that's how they referred to it when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: From this area, how far is -- that is, if you can tell us, how far was the building that you called Vinko Martinovic's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Next to the line, you mean? Well, I'm not sure. I never thought about it. But it could be about a kilometre away. I can't really say, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you exactly reconstruct your movements on that day, the 17th of September, 1993, when you left Heliodrom, from that moment up to the moment when you put on the uniforms in Vinko Martinovic's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Why, yes. Dinko came to fetch us that morning, called us out. We did. We mounted the truck. Then we took the road across Zovnica, because there were four men working on a private house. They had been working there from before. Because one knew that the four of them had to go there, so we went first to Zovnica, left them there, and the rest of us were then taken to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After we arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We were lined up straight away, and then Mr. Vinko, he said to that Ernest to assign four men. He ordered him to take four men, and he made his pick, took them to the basement, and told them to put on many-coloured uniforms that had already been brought there by I think somebody called Gvaro. He had one arm crippled - that is, he only had a thumb - and he brought them as we stood by the wall. And then those uniforms were put on and came out, and then he gave them those wooden rifles. And when he gave them the wooden rifles, Enes Pajo passed out, fainted, and Stela then shouted, "Well, undress him. Why do I need him?" and then said, "Well, give me another one." And that's how it was. Ernest then assigned me, made me put on his uniform, and gave me a wooden rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where did you put on that rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any patches on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, nothing special. It was just a camouflage uniform, such as was worn by HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have any special armbands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, there was nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did those wooden rifles look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: They looked like those automatic rifles except that they had wooden butts. That is, dark brown painted over the previous night, and they were painted by Mr. Semir Edic, called Daka, from Stolac. He was the one who painted them with his own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Because that's where I worked the day before, and when I returned from the automobile club, he was in the process of painting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was it obvious that the rifles were wooden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, you know what is a wooden rifle and what is a real rifle. I do think there is a difference. I mean, I personally had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You mean it was obvious that those were fake rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: But of course they were fake rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I say, of course they were fake rifles, seeing that they were wooden. I personally carried one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How did you do that? In what way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, in my hands, like I would a real rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But you could have it on your shoulder.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know Halid Jazvin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Halid Jazvin. I do. I mean, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see him that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really know him all that well at that time. I came to know him much better when we crossed over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see him that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I told you already that at that time I didn't really know him all that well and that I came to know him better when we crossed over to the side under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you remember seeing him that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Oh, that? No, I don't. All I remember is some individuals. I can give you their names, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's not necessary, thank you. And where did you move before you reached the building of what you call -- told us was emergency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Where we went from the headquarters towards the Rondo, and then from Rondo in the direction of the emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you walk unobstructed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did anyone lead you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Ernest led -- drove us in a yellow van which was half truck, half van, and it had a POM mounted on it, an anti-aircraft machine-gun.
