utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you sure it was a van? Could it be a jeep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, no, no. It wasn't a jeep. What we call it is Fico van, Zastava van.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that part of the street where the building of the emergency is, was there a cord across the street with sandbags over it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: There was a wall which we made of sandbags. That is, we filled bags with earth and then built that wall across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you point at its location on the -- on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't. Just a moment. Here, from this building, from that corner there to the corner of this building over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please mark that. If, that is, we shall be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Like this, in this direction, this is the top of this building, and this is the foot of the building so that you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And can you put "3" next to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can, yes. I'll put it here so that you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us what is it that you marked with number 3 so that we have your statement in the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That is a wall across the road made of bags, and on it there were two or three rifle nests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Vinko Martinovic was in the basement of the emergency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please describe the cellar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, cellar, like is -- a cellar is a cellar. You go down the steps and there is a room there, right below. As soon as we had come down those stairs, he met us there and told us what our task would be, what we were to do and how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was there any furniture there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, there were some hospital affairs, I mean things that usually belong to a hospital, some cupboards or wardrobes or some hospital beds or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that this was the hospital inventory there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I can't say what was there. It had evidently been put in there. But what had been there before, because I didn't know the building before, of course you can bring in anything anywhere. I know what I saw there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did it look to you like a military command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I mean that basement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. It is simply that the line was there and simply happened to be there, and that's what it was called simply. But during the war, it did not house a military hospital or any command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did Vinko Martinovic tell you exactly? Did he make any promises? Did he promise that he'd help you go abroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: First he asked us who we were, where we came from, and then he told us what would our duty be. And I've already told you about that. If need be, I'll repeat it all, right to the end. And after that, he said, "And if all this is done, then I guarantee that you will be allowed to go within 48 hours, to go home, abroad, or if you feel like it, join my unit." And this was then confirmed by his soldiers, that he was in a position to keep his promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did you answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any answer. How -- what all we had in our heads was death, in view of the task given us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain it to us? Why is it that death was in your heads? Did Vinko Martinovic threaten you with death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, he didn't threaten us, but when he was telling us what our task would be, there is nothing else you can expect but head straight for your death, because we were about to be used as human shields. Since they didn't know where exactly the soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were, they wanted them to start firing at us so that they could see where that fire came from and so that their soldiers could respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did this mean that you were a human shield and markers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, that's what a human shield is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was anybody hiding behind your bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Hiding? There was a group of soldiers behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How many of them? Wait a moment because of the transcript. How far behind you was this group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Not more than a few metres, not much of a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, perhaps five metres, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And were those soldiers equally exposed to danger as the four of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: They were coming after us. They were behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, well, right. Let's go back to the photograph. And show us, please, on the photograph which was the direction that you took.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Just a moment. This was an access path. Then from here, because a tank was coming here, and we waited for the tank until it fetched up there, and then we took this road, and they stayed behind. And we walked here and here. Then went around this fountain, across the Bulevar, came to this side here near the pavement, on this side, which was manned by the Bosnia -- BH army, and that is where we took to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, let's please stop. Will you now mark, but with a dotted line, the route which you followed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: With dotted line or just plain dots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Now, this is black and white and I'm not sure whether one can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please speak up when you're saying this because --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm saying that this is all black and white and this is black, and there is a fountain here. I'm not sure one can see that. This is how we walked. And now, whether it's somewhere here, I think it is to this side, which the Armija held, near the pavement, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And now, will you put number 4 next to this route.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Can I do it here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let us go back to your -- to that situation when you were, as you put it, a human shield. You have some military experience; we agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how is it that the four of you represented a human shield for ten or so soldiers moving five metres behind you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Fine. We walk in front of them and because we are walking in a line, one behind the other, and of course they will fire at the one who is in front. If you are moving in a column, then, don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I'm explaining it to you as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not waving at you. Don't get offended.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not getting offended. I'm just telling you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And in a way you've already answered my next question, but I nevertheless want to make it quite clear. You were moving in a goose line, one by one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us exactly in which order did the four of you move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, what was the exact file, I can't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you the first one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps the last one in that file?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really know. I mean, where was who at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But behind the last one of the four of you comes the column of HVO soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And was there -- between the first soldier in that column and the last one in your file, was there -- were there five metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The first one, no, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I didn't get really your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is addressing the other counsel and says, "I didn't hear it quite well."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear it quite well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the question? Because I didn't figure it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I didn't really hear the witness and I wasn't following the transcript. I do not know what the transcript says. Does it say that between the last soldier and the four who, as the witness says, were the human soldiers, that is the last one in the human shield and the first soldier in the HVO file, was the distance between them five metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I also have the headset on over my ears. So will you please be precise. We are wasting time if I have to repeat my questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, yes, but we must make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As you're moving in that file, as you were moving in that file, was there any firing then? Did anyone fire at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. There was no fire until before we crossed. Or rather, we had already run across, and we were already, for the most part, on the side with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were still behind the fountain. And as soon as the first bullet was fired, we simply went down to the ground and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, whether you were at all a human shield when there was no shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can say that I was a human shield, of course I was, because there were shelling before that. All this happened, then came a tank. All this was preplanned, and it was normal to expect the shooting would start. We just ran across. They didn't see us. They saw someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were faster than the bullet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was not faster than the bullet. Because as soon as the first shot was fired, we threw ourselves on to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you reveal the positions of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: As we lay on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As you were moving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: How could I discover it when there was no shooting or anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you personally protect anyone with your body from the fire, from the bullets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I did not, because we were all lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But you just said that you were not lying on the ground all the time, that you were moving. I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was saying that I was moving until the first shot was fired. As soon as the first shot was fired, we threw ourselves on the ground. At that moment, I understood that you were asking me whether we were lying down when this went on. Was that your question? And did I protect anyone as I lay down? That is how I understood your question. And I answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So you continue to allege that you were in a human shield, though that human shield, as you -- the term you use, did not fulfil its purpose as there was no shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: What do you mean there was no shooting? We were exposed to crossfire throughout the attack. Of course it was a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about the moment when you were heading towards the separation line and as you were crossing that separation line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You're asking me whether I was as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seric, I think that the witness has answered according to his perception and understanding of the facts. If you don't agree with that, everyone will understand that, but these are conclusions and not questions. So please be kind enough to put questions to the witness and that will make us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Mr. Fourmy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: To go back to the tank -- I'm trying to formulate the question so that I cannot be said to be using conclusions. Who was the first who reached the wall of sandbags, you or the tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We were brought there from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see how the tank reached the sandbag wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You mean how it got there? It came from the direction of the Rondo and we had already been transferred from the emergency basement to this side entrance to the building and we were waiting with this group, and when we saw it coming from the direction of the Rondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. Did you see the way in which the tank reached up to the sandbag wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. I'm telling you that it came from the direction of the Rondo to the sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the tank did not pass through the sandbags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: When it got there, to the sandbags, they had already been removed when it arrived. This was done by the others. They -- the other manpower who were there, they had removed the sandbags. And then he fired three or four shells from that position, and then it moved on, and our task was, when it reached us, that we should accompany it to the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let's go slowly because, after all, this is a military operation and we need to analyse it in detail, and thereby elucidate your personal role and the role of the prisoners in that military operation. As I was saying, please look at the photograph. You have marked on the photograph the wall made out of sandbags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, were the four of you going alongside that tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: While it was standing up there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: At any time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We went alongside it after it had fired three or four shells, when the artillery -- the shelling had stopped, this went on for about 15 or 20 minutes, I don't know exactly. Then the tank --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. This is a cross-examination, not the direct examination. So I'm asking you once again: Where was the tank when it fired the first few shells? Was it next to -- had it reached the sandbags or had it passed the sandbag wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It had reached the sandbags here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: And it fired the shells from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where were you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In this building, at the side entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What happened then, according to what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After that, the tank came down the road, as we were told it would, it reached us, and then we came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Show us now where the tank was when you came out to this clearing, this crossroads.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Here, you mean? When we went alongside it, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was it going with you all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It came here, and we were waiting here for it to come. As soon as it arrived, we started running out. It went down this way and reached this spot, and we ran across this way. As soon as the first bullet was fired, we threw ourselves on the ground, and that is how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: For the record, will you please tell us: What was the route the tank took?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It took this route up to this crossroads, the intersection with the Bulevar. Here. It didn't go out onto the intersection itself. There was a stop sign there. So it went as far as this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So when we reconstruct the route the tank took, and your column, did you part from the tank when you took the path alongside the emergency building, to the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: That is what we were told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We had to run. We had to cross this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The time you spent moving alongside the tank, were you protected by this white building which you call the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: From this side, until we reached this corner, we were protected, but we were not protected from any fire that might come from this side, because the front went on. The line went on down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Precisely that is why I'm asking you: Did the tank accompany you to protect you or were you moving to protect someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We weren't protecting anyone. Actually, we were protecting these soldiers who were coming behind us. We couldn't protect the tank. It was protecting us. It was supporting us, in a sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Is it logical, on the basis of your own knowledge of the rules of war, for the infantry to protect tanks, or is it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It depends on the circumstances. Though I'm not a military strategist and I don't wish to go into that much, but I think one protects the other. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you reached the cellar, the basement of the emergency building, did Brada come with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, we came with him. He brought us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did he tell Vinko Martinovic that you had volunteered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He just handed us over to Vinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your examination-in-chief by the Prosecution that he used a term "extremists" to describe you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Extremists, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know what he had in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, you can make your own conclusions as to what the word "extremists" means. It's not a nice word? Is it a nice word or an ugly word?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Those wooden rifles, did they have any belts, straps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All four of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How were the barrels made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In the same shape as normal rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any small wooden planks and shaped in the form of a real rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, modelled on a real Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So an artist must have produced it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know who made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did the four of you previously come to an agreement to flee to the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: There was no discussion. We were just -- we kept quiet, waiting for what the future would bring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As you were moving and crossing the separation line, that is, the Bulevar, did you see anyone getting killed in the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone getting wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This man with me, Tucakovic, he had some small shrapnel on his back. I also had a small shrapnel on my shoulder blade and I had a cut on my head, and they never found a shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly when the wounding occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: While this exchange of fire was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where were you then? Let's go back to the photograph. Where exactly were you when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Here, the place where I had marked, when we threw ourselves on the ground. And we didn't move throughout, throughout the attack, the exchange of fire, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you wounded while you were moving or while you were lying down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: While I was lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any prisoner volunteered to participate in the HVO operation on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have those wooden rifles on you all the time as you were moving, lying down, and running, and crossing the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. I carried it across myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what happened to it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I gave it to a little boy of 4 or 5. I gave it to him as a toy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did the rifle look like a toy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Our children make rifles of that kind as toys.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions more for you and then we'll be through. In the course of your deposition today, you said that on a number of occasions you came to work, and you showed us the various locations, and that there was shooting. You even showed us where the unit or the soldiers of the BH army were located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Why was it necessary, if you as a prisoner knew that, why was it necessary for the HVO soldiers to find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I'll be glad to. You stated that you personally were aware where these soldiers of the BH army were along the separation line. How is it possible, then, that the HVO soldiers didn't know that, and they needed to use you to reveal their positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Everyone knew roughly which building they were in, but they didn't know exactly the position, and that is why they used us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you explain in greater detail what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: You mean the exact position of the bunker or the rifles? Because a building is big, and you have to be able to assess exactly where the rifle is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Is that important for a tank driver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In this case, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the calibre of the cannon that a tank has and the destructive power of a shell fired by a tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I think they were 55-calibre tanks, the projectiles that they fired. That's how we referred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What is the destructive power of such a projectile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can that projectile destroy three or four windows at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, microphone, please. I'm sorry. We didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seric, the witness is not a military expert. He is here to depose about what he knows, information at his disposal. So if you want to have an expert to come here to explain the destructive power of a tank, whether it can destroy one or several windows, what is the impact of such a tank on the members of the BH army who may have been in the building, very well, but not today. This cross-examination has been going on for an hour and a half, whereas examination-in-chief took one hour, one minute. So I must remind you that that was not the agreement we reached; that the two should correspond. I see that I'm speaking too fast, and I apologise to the interpreters. I haven't finished. I understand that this may be difficult, Mr. Seric, and I see that you're doing everything you can to make your questions as simple and as precise as possible, but I have the impression that we haven't learnt much. I really would like us to complete the deposition of this witness this morning, and we have been going on for an hour and a half, so it will be rather difficult for us to complete him before the break. Mr. Seric, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm almost done, and you're quite right, but as the witness was testifying about something very important that my client is being charged with -- he was telling us about his subjective feeling and not about the actual fact. So if he was used for any purpose, he may have been used as a marker - and I'm now using military terminology, not the terminology of the witness - and he himself tells us that he felt as if he was a human shield. That is why I asked him on what those feelings are based. But be that as it may, let's go on. I think Madam Registrar has already given a number to this Defence exhibit with the markings of the witness, so we would like to tender that into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you -- yes, D2/3. Is that right, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I just confer briefly with my client, just for a second?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will allow it, exceptionally. You know that is not the custom, but please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you. That ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Seric. Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any additional questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A very few, Mr. Fourmy. I'm confident that we can conclude before the break. If the witness -- I don't know if the witness still has -- if I can request, please, the colour copy of Exhibit 14.5. If that could just be put on the ELMO please. It's not going to be a detailed examination. Mr. Fourmy, I'd like to think this won't be disputed, and I hope it won't be, but just so the record is perfectly clear, let me put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, this photograph, I take it you can see that the building that you referred to as the emergency, or the middle, the most prominent building in the middle of the photograph, roughly to the right of the fountain area. You can see that building, can you not? Do you see that, sir? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, there are other buildings, including that building, other buildings around it, just in the general photograph. Do you see a number of buildings that appear to be freshly painted, quite bright colours: bright pink, bright white? Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, sir, was that the condition of all these buildings in the summer of 1993, or were in fact many of these buildings much more damaged than what they appear in this photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This part here was damaged. Now it has all been renovated. It was renovated now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. That's the only point on that item that I just wanted to be clear. Now, you say that these rifles, these wooden rifles, were -- I think the word counsel used was "obvious," it was obvious that they were fake rifles. Now, let's be clear about this. Was it obvious to you, as a trained soldier, when you held it in your own hands, that it was not in fact a real weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Of course. They were just wooden rifles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, whether or not it might have appeared either obviously fake or in fact like a real weapon if viewed from 100 to 200 metres away?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question emphatically, because the witness could not be outside his own body 200 metres away to be able to see himself with the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, the witness is a soldier. He was asked this on cross-examination. This is fair redirect and it's a fair question this witness can answer. Let me rephrase it, if it will assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were a trained soldier that operated in the field for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some long period of time. Can you just please tell those of us -- all of us in the Chamber, how do you think the rifle that you were carrying that day, how would that rifle have appeared from approximately 100 to 200 metres away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It would appear like a real one, and just then, you wouldn't have to be even at that distance to think it was a real one. Even if you were closer, you would think it was a real one, because these are seconds in question, when you don't have time to judge whether it's a real one or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Witness J, a final two questions. You've been asked by counsel whether truly in fact you were at risk during this situation. Let me just understand, sir. You were forced to advance in front of an HVO unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact as a result of that, both you and Mr. Tucakovic - and I apologise for my pronunciation - both of you were wounded during this incident, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, thank you. Witness J, your deposition has been completed. You have seen that sometimes we have rather lively debates, but it is due to the quality of the information that the witnesses bring, so that each party wishes to make the best of that information. So this only shows that this will be extremely interesting for the judges, that you came to The Hague and I thank you for it very much. You will now be able to return home and I wish you a safe journey to your country of residence. Please don't move. Thank you. Please don't move until the usher escorts you out. We will meet again at 2.00 p.m. to continue our deposition hearings. The hearing is adjourned. Goodbye, Witness J.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The session is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Prosecutor, can we have the next witness, please. And do you need any protection measures for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fourmy. The witness who is called to testify now has requested face image distortion and pseudonym, as most of our witnesses already had here, for reasons well already known here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Registrar, can you please prepare a pseudonym? Oh, I see that's already done. So, Usher, will you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness K.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. How long do you think the examination-in-chief will take you, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will try to complete my task somewhere around one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. You asked for protection measures so that you will have your facial distortion for the public, and on the monitors your image will be scrambled, and a pseudonym. Your pseudonym will be Witness K, so do not feel upset if we address you only in that manner, Witness K, all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you begin with your deposition, I should like to ask you to make the solemn declaration, the text of which the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness K. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try to put yourself at ease, make yourself as comfortable as possible. The microphones are rather powerful, so that you do not have to come too close to microphones to speak. The usher will now show you a sheet of paper with a name on it, and you simply have to look at this sheet of paper and tell me if it is your name on the paper, but do not say it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The usher will now show this document to both sides. The procedure that is applied here is as follows: First the Prosecutor will ask you some questions; then it will be the turn of the Defence; and then if the Prosecutor wishes to do so, he may also ask you some additional questions. We shall also make a break after an hour and a half or an hour and 20 minutes, but if I understand well, thanks to the Prosecutor, it will be after he has finished asking you his questions. So unless you have some questions, I will give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness K. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, you now have the floor for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. K, just some questions relevant to your background. You're a Bosniak Muslim, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you belong to any military ABiH formation in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where did your unit hold the lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In the village of Rotimlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of tasks did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Our task was the defence against the Serb aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any tensions between the ABiH and HVO at that time? I mean the time when you had to resist the Serbs' aggression.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, no tension to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And when did these tensions become reality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The tensions became a reality when the arrests started, and that was around the -- around June, or rather before that, in Mostar, when the conflict broke out between those two components of the Armija and the HVO, and this also in part found its reflection in our relations, and as the time went on, the tensions grew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you ever arrested during the war in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 13th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It happened in the village of Rotimlja, or rather the place, the locality, the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was your unit involved in combat at that time? I mean the time when you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. There was no combat at that time. I didn't have even any weapons on me at the moment of my arrest. Our unit was to leave the area. However, HVO unit intercepted us and captured us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why was your unit to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We were to leave the area because major HVO forces had stationed there, and in order to avoid an armed conflict, we had to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did soldiers in your unit put some resistance when you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What military rank did you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There were no ranks at the time. I was just a plain soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any commissioned and non-commissioned officers in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, no. There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did your commander have any military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Our commander did not have a rank. We did not address him by any rank. At that time, our commander had already been arrested by then, and kept in the Gabela prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who arrested you? I mean, which unit, which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Which units? HVO units, or rather, units which had arm -- insignia with the letters HVO. And in conversations, and because we recognised some of the soldiers, they were known as Bozan's men. That was a unit belonging to the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was in command of that unit? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Battalion was Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where were you taken after the arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There, in that place when we were arrested, we were taken to a room, to a place in Rotimlja, a building which housed their command, and after a while we were taken to the Gabela camp. I spent -- I was in the Gabela camp until the evening of the same day, but then again, that very evening, I was moved over to the Heliodrom camp in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you registered on arrival to Gabela and Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Registered by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I mean by the people who were running these facilities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, not in Gabela. Nobody registered us there. And when we reached Heliodrom, no, not there again. I don't know that anyone registered us. They simply put us in the premises of the central prison, and it was only later on that the Red Cross registered us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you interviewed by some people running the Heliodrom about your military background, your status?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. Nobody conducted any interview with me. We were in that group which was brought and put the first night in solitary confinement, and the rest of the time, that is, about 20 days, in the basement. Nobody conducted any official interview with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know which unit was running Heliodrom at that time? Unit or formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The prison was run by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why do you think so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, I think so because the military police had their insignia which said "HVO Military Police," and they also had white belts and the bandolier over their camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of Heliodrom at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I am not absolutely sure, but I think that in the beginning it was -- that one of the commanders was a man called Tomo Sokota. I don't know who succeeded him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you spell his name, please, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: First, first name, and full name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: T-o-m-o. That is the first name. And the last name, S-, with a diacritic mark, -o-k-o-t-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you explained to us that first you were kept for some period of time in the basement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they keep all people taken from Rotimlja together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: All of us who were brought then, yes, we were put in the same basement, plus the others who were being brought, those who had stayed behind in that village, I mean, villagers, the civilians. They were also put together with us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When were you registered by the Red Cross? While you were kept in the basement, or later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The Red Cross registered us whilst we were in the basement, but they did not do it in the basement. They had taken us to a room on an upper floor to be registered there by the Red Cross. And as soon as that was over, they took us back immediately. That happened on the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any other prisoners kept in Heliodrom at that time, apart from your, let's say, soldier-mate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit about other prisoners kept in Heliodrom at the time, both in the basement and in other areas where you were taken later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Right. While we were in the basement, we could only look through the keyhole or through some small cracks in the door. We could see some men walking up and down the passage, because not far from where we were kept was the kitchen, so that we could see a large number of men kept there, imprisoned there. And later on, when we were transferred to an upper floor, to rooms on an upper floor, we were in a large passage where there were -- leading into three or four rooms, and all one of them were full [as interpreted]. One of them, one of those rooms, was the room where prisoners were kept, I mean prisoners who had committed some transgressions - I don't know - those who had refused to go to the front line or something like that, that is, members of the HVO and some others who had committed some crimes in town or somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because they would come from their room to our room, and they also -- and would also ill-treat us and take valuables that we had, that one could see, so that -- and this ill-treatment consisted of -- they also sang a lot and made us sing for them, and they even made a band of us, the prisoners there, and came to call it the Blue Band, Plavi Orkestar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why did they call you the Blue Band?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We were called Blue Band, I guess, because of the kind of uniforms we wore, because we had arrived there in military, or rather, camouflage uniforms. They gave us a different uniform. They gave us uniforms that were formerly worn by the former army, or rather, cadets who were stationed there, who lived there at the Heliodrom as they underwent training.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see female prisoners in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Women were also -- there was a group of women who were imprisoned in Heliodrom. They were upstairs in the loft of the building, in the attic of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Can you say just a few words about the conditions of life for prisoners in Heliodrom? I mean food, water, other facilities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were far from normal. We had two meals, rather meagre, water. On a number of occasions, there would be a sufficient quantity. Our accommodation as such was practically none because the space was just too small and there were too many people for any decent accommodation, so that some -- there were some 60 metres square and there would be 62 or 3 men perhaps in one such room. And on only one occasion did we have -- or rather, were left without water or food for 48 hours. It happened, I don't know, there was a battle somewhere or something, and so I guess this was done in punishment, to punish us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know anything about military units deployed in Heliodrom area and Heliodrom itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There were some units at the Heliodrom itself. I, of course, have no way of knowing which units exactly and what they were called, but I know that often a large number of troops would come in or go out beneath our windows. There were even two tanks stationed below the prison. And in the vicinity of Heliodrom, to the north, there was also a unit stationed, and I believe it was the 9th Battalion. There was yet another unit called Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Inside Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Inside, inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Tigers. Do you know what kind of unit was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It was a unit, what shall I call it? I don't really know, whether -- well, we guessed it was the Croatian army, but what its tasks were, I -- I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why do you think that they were from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The prisoners, those who worked for the Tigers, and also those who went to the locality of Buna, to Thunders, to Gromovi, that was another unit, which was part of the Croatian army, and these Gromovi or Thunders, they were the artillery. They were using mortars. And the prisoners talked to those men and those men then told them that they came from some places in Croatia, that is from the Sava valley or places from around Rijeka, Split, and other places, and this is how we concluded that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right. Did they ever take you outside the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For what purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The purpose was to take us for forced labour, to fortify the lines, make trenches, make transfer trenches, transfer sandbags, digging the graves, burying the dead, carry the food, fell trees or chop wood, or so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever volunteer to do this job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I never volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember in which locations of Heliodrom -- sorry, you performed this, as you called it, forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I do remember the locations. Starting from Balinovac, Pasinovac, the Bulevar, Santic street, Rastani, Dzubrani, Vojno, the aviation bridge, the airport and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Let's start with the areas of Mostar. Did you know Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did know it, so-so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Among the locations you were taken to perform forced labour, you just named Santiceva street and Bulevar. Do you remember any --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: -- specific -- sorry, let me complete my question. Do you remember any specific incidents associated with these two areas, I mean Santiceva street -- let's begin with Santiceva street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I remember incidents. Let's start with the Santiceva street. I remember once when we had to push a car full of explosives to a building in which it was assumed the army, Armija, had positions. We were lined up behind a garage wall, and a group of five or six men that were pushing this vehicle towards the building, from the building, fire was opened, quite normally, and people were injured. But regardless of that, as we were lined up against the garage wall, as a man fell, being wounded, a new man had to join the group to push, and this lasted for some ten or 15 minutes. And then, in the end, they gave up on the idea. I also remember another incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Let's complete this incident. Did you participate himself [sic] pushing on this car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I did not participate because I was still waiting in the line behind the garage wall. It still wasn't my turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. I saw it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners wounded on that day on Santiceva street while you were performing that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, there were prisoners wounded. I remember one was a professor, I don't remember his name. He was seriously wounded. I don't even know whether he survived. I don't know what happened to him after that. There were some others who were wounded. Whether they were taken to the emergency ward and whether they were given any emergency treatment, I can't tell you, because at the end of this operation, we were separated from those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned some other incidents on Santiceva street.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor -- excuse me, Witness K. Mr. Prosecutor, if there is a series of incidents, I don't know whether it would be useful for the transcript, and especially for the continuation, to ask the witness for at least the approximate date of each of those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It is hard to give you a date because, in moments such as these, in the course of our days as captives, one didn't even know the date, but this can only be estimated. I know that it was maybe sometime in the first half of July, something like that, and then afterwards, again, after mid-August until September, so somewhere there, around those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed with the second incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The second incident also occurred with our group in the Santiceva street, or rather Celovina, when a group was emptying fire extinguishing devices and another group was filling those empty devices with explosives, fuses and explosives. We did this all day long. So that as soon as darkness started to fall, we went to the front lines, or rather the line held by the HVO forces, to see the positions of the opposing side, that is the army, and then they would indicate to us the key points where we had to go later and throw those explosives with the fuse lit. So once it got really dark, we would reach those places with the fuses lit. We would cross to the other side of the street because, in fact, there was just a street separating the warring sides, and we would throw those explosives over. And once we had done that, we had to go back to the initial position because we were threatened if one did not return, the rest of the group would be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned confrontation line or front line. Do you remember which are the areas of Mostar belonged to confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the whole town and where the line was. It went inclusive -- from inclusive, at the southern end, Semovac, or rather the bridge on Radobolja [phoen], and then if you were to draw a line to an old shop selling car parts, I think it was held by Herzegovina Auto, and then straight on towards the fountain at the Bulevar, and then from that fountain again a line. All this followed the road. As I was saying, from the fountain towards the old secondary school, the -- or grammar school. Then the bank, then behind the Hit, and then it went down from Hit towards the post office and Santiceva street. So that in Santiceva street, there was the area around the customs bridge. That is as far as I went. So Celovina and the area towards the Neretva river. That would be roughly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the way the line was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know which unit or units were in charge of the confrontation line, or some areas of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There were several units, in my opinion. And as I went to work and while actually working, one could hear the names of some of those units. One could even read some graffiti on the walls, and to conclude from them which units they were. For instance, I know that there was Benko Penavic; that was one unit. Then I know there was an ATG, anti-terrorist group. Then there was a convicts unit. Then a name we heard most often was a group under Stela. Then in Santiceva street, there was a gentleman I think he was called Zele. He was I think one of the commanders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fourmy, I would like to go into a private session for some minutes because our witness now can give names of some people which can reveal his identity and also reveal the identity of these people which the point is not desirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you ever taken to perform forced labour in other locations than in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Outside of town I went to the village of Rastani and the village of Vojno, and I also mentioned the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Vojno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I stayed in Vojno for under a month. I think this was the end of July until about the 20th, or maybe earlier than that, the 20th of August. As I said, I can't tell you the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was in command of this facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: You mean in Vojno?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Vojno.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: At first, when I arrived there, there was no one among the important people there. But judging by the attitudes they took, I think it was a gentleman called Sunjic or Rudo Ramic. I'm afraid I can't say for sure. But later, Mihalj came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where were you taken to perform some kind of labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I went to Rastani twice to do forced labour. Once I went there for one day and once I spent a couple of days there, and we slept in a silo which used to store grain before, where grain used to be stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember when were you taken to Rastani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I was taken to Rastani after an HVO operation which had been carried out against the army, and I was then taken -- I can't say what date it was. It could have been sometime in September. I don't know for sure. Anyway, we were taken there in order to dig trenches and to fortify the line that had been reached as a result of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any villagers in Rastani while performing forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. In Rastani I didn't see any civilians, and the houses had been burnt down, so that I didn't notice any civilians in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right. When were you released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I was released from the Heliodrom on the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The International Red Cross arrived and said that things had been agreed, that there would be release of prisoners, detainees, whatever you wish to call them. And through the mediation of the International Red Cross, this exchange was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And my last question, just to clarify: Could you repeat the name of the Croatian army that was deployed in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They were the Tigrovi, or Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Fourmy, I have completed my direct examination ten minutes ahead of time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. I think that if I try very hard, I could contradict you by saying that you have spared nine minutes and I don't know how many seconds, and I am very grateful to you for it. Mr. Krsnik or Mr. Seric. I don't know in which order you wish to proceed. Perhaps Mr. Krsnik first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Let me introduce myself. I'm attorney Krsnik and I represent the accused Mladen Naletilic. I have a few questions for you. I will speak slowly, and please wait for me to finish because of the interpretation. And I shall try and phrase my questions so that you can give me brief and concise answers: "yes," "no," "I don't know." That is what I shall try to do in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps go into private session for the first couple of minutes? I won't take long in general, but maybe to begin with I might enter the area of some identification particulars, so could we have a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, yes, please. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the Gabela camp run by somebody called Boko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And is he a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know whose member he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did military police search you when you entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Whether it was the military police or somebody else, I was searched at the time of arrest and at the time of arrival in Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did they have white belts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That is what you said about Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: About Heliodrom, yes, I can give you information. And as for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the security unit at the Heliodrom, did they have patches on their sleeves saying VP -- MP, military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They had badges which said HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The Tigers, do you know anything about that unit, or is it only that you heard stories about it from somebody else, from other co-prisoners or whatever you call them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that through the window that I saw men wearing patches of the Tigers, but other people worked for them, so they will know more about them than I personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I could only observe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So did you see a Tiger or what or the lettering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I couldn't really see the inscription.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And what about the Gromovi, about Thunders; you only heard about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yeah. I heard about it from my colleagues who were with me, and they also will tell you more about them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You personally don't know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you do not have any personal knowledge again because you mentioned this Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know where it was? You said it was stationed somewhere in the town. Is it that you personally know or from stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, I worked in that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That was between -- now, how shall I explain it? As you come down the Bulevar to Rondo and then to Balinovac, in that part of the street, that is where the unit, I think Benko Penavic, and then an ATG group, and -- but they were called -- or rather, what we called them, Stela's men, and then they said one of those, one of those was the Convicts Battalion. I cannot attribute this name to that unit and another name to another unit. That is what I heard, through people talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So it was just through talking and stories and it is in these streets that you just mentioned, it was positions over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is conversing with his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you perhaps show it on the map where that could be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course I could do it. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I didn't think to do this but I'm coming to the end. This is my final, my last question, Mr. Fourmy, because I was quite happy with this answer because all this is based on hearsay. Mr. Usher, will you please help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no English translation] ... a larger photograph. I'm sorry. I did understand the drift of your question a moment ago and perhaps you will need a larger photograph for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am very familiar with Mostar. I know the streets that the witness is talking about. So it's all here but as I said it's all based on hearsay so this is just an additional minor verification so this is the end. I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The part where those units were stationed was there. No, I'm asking about the Convicts Battalion, the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I heard about it from those soldiers. I cannot say that which is the Convicts Battalion and which is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we are talking about. I'm not putting words in your mouth. I'm just saying you heard it from other people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy, since this is the end of my cross-examination and my last question, and I understand what is the origin of those stories, so I will not ask any further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness K, can you perhaps show it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, this is not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You don't think it's clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you rather use a colour photograph, the same photograph but in colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be all right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 14.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Rondo is up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, you are following -- you are moving in a good direction. You're getting warmer. The Rondo is up there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, tell us roughly, where was this Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, this is not a good enough photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm offering you a better photograph, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I used this photograph owing to the good services of the Prosecution, but here we have a larger photograph, a photograph covering a larger area.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14.3/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how about this photograph? Can you find your way around this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Somewhere here, somewhere there. It was on a corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As you go down that street from Rondo towards Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, no, no. Towards Balinovac, towards Balinovac. And there, on the corner, was one command station, and I think that was Mr. Stela's command, and across the street was yet another command which had a graffiti there saying Benko Penavic. And it was there -- now, whether this was the official name or not, but they were saying, "We're the Convicts' Battalion," we're this, we're that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So it is somewhere in this part, in that area near Stela's command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I do not have any further questions, Mr. Fourmy. Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. And it is sometimes very difficult to control the situation to the very end, but then I would like to suggest that we benefit from the end of this part of cross-examination and to make our break now, to resume at a quarter to 4.00, at 1545. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Par, I'm sorry. Do you know how long your cross-examination will take, so that the Prosecutor could know? If it would be very short, if you will have only a few questions, then perhaps we could have a witness -- then the Prosecution could have another witness ready. It's only to help the Prosecutor to organise better. As you know, tomorrow we have to break at lunch-time, so that perhaps we could -- Yes, please, do sit down, I'm saying to the witness. Perhaps with the interpreters' cooperation, perhaps we could work for an extra five minutes, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy, I've already told our learned friends that this cross-examination will take about 15 to 20 minutes; at least, that is what I expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you from the bottom of my heart, Mr. Par. Witness K, it will now be the second Defence team which will ask you some questions. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness K, I'm Zelimir Par, a lawyer and one of the co-counsel for Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela. Before I move on to some other questions which have to do with the incident that you told us about today, I'd like to ascertain a few other things with the help of these photographs, to try to make sure of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the usher please put Exhibit 14.5 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I simply cannot see it properly on this photograph, so that I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether the witness could identify the place where he was brought on the day that Stela beat a prisoner. The witness complained that the photograph was not clear enough to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But I can describe it to you what it looked like. Let's see. If you cannot identify that place on this photograph, if you do not find your way around this photograph, tell us so: "I can't find my way around, I cannot identify the place, I do not know."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. I simply don't -- can't figure it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know the area that was under Stela's responsibility, the area of responsibility of Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, a part of it, a part of that area, was as you came down the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No. You don't have to go into that. Just say -- do you know or do you not know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I know a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you show it on this map or can't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It is next to this fountain here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If you are showing it, then do it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It's around the fountain here, this part here, around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then let us not mark this, but note for the record that the witness pointed at the area around the fountain, in front of a facility called --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You will tell us. The fountain is in front of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The fountain is on the street called Bulevar, at the turning to the upper part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But do you know what this building next to the fountain is called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I don't, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. Never mind. So we do not need the photograph any more. Thank you very much. We shall not need it any more. Witness K, let us then go back to that day which you described when you met Stela. What day was it, what period of time, what segment of time? Can you identify it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date but that was sometime in July, I'd say, sometime up to the 10th of July, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see. Up to the 10th of July. And you say that you arrived with a group of prisoners. Can you give us the names of some of the prisoners that were with you in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, the names are in my statement, in the statement that I've -- that I gave to the people from The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness K, you are here a witness testifying before this Court, before this Tribunal, and therefore you should tell us that. Is there any reason why you do not want or cannot give us the names of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Par, excuse me, I'm sorry, but if you want to make it easier for the witness to answer, perhaps we could go into private session for a few minutes, if you think that might help.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy, thank you. My question had to do with the names of prisoners who were -- who could have arrived with the witness that day to that place. I do not know why should the names of these prisoners be a secret and especially I see no reason to do that in a private session. Of course, I do not know what the Prosecutor thinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
